Instead of feeding LLMs 34: disconnected prompts, an MCP-powered ODI server acts as the "brain" of customer 35: needs — letting agents invent, evaluate, and ideate solutions anchored in 36: verified, measurable customer outcomes (Job Maps, Desired Outcomes, and 37: Opportunity Scores). 38: 39: This repository is an experimental testbed for understanding server–client MCP 40: communication streams, built on [`FastMCP`](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp). 41: 42: We don't publish dates. This page changes when the code does. 43: 44: **Project site:** the site lives at 45: **[alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi](https://alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi/)**, 46: with a documentation hub at 47: **[alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi/docs/](https://alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi/docs/)**. 48: It is republished by the `Pages` workflow on every push to `main`. Persists to SQLite by default. | 70: | **`apps/studio-api/`** | `agentic-odi-studio-api` | FastAPI **Living Studio sidecar**. Serves config, health, canvas data, local mutations, MCP passthrough, SSE chat, conversation history, and the PM memory store, plus the built SPA. | 71: | **`apps/cli/`** | `agentic-odi-cli` | Typer CLI with interactive chat plus full entity CRUD, `schema`, `connectors`, and local-first (`--backend local`) or remote (`--backend mcp`) data access. | 72: | **`apps/studio/`** | React + TypeScript + Vite | **The Living Studio** SPA and Tauri 2 desktop shell. For the desktop app, use 101: `npm --prefix apps/studio run tauri dev`. See 102: [Running The Living Studio](docs/living-studio.md). 103: 104: The first time you open the Studio, the tour asks what you want to win: an 105: opportunity you already have in mind, a priority your boss handed you, finding 106: the next opportunity, or pressure-testing a bet. Pick one and the conversation 107: starts there — no form, no framework speech. It still asks for your product and 108: audience when it needs them, and everything you say is optional and skippable. 109: 110: After that it opens as one room: the transcript and the composer never leave the 111: screen. Describe a job or a customer frustration, or type `/` for commands that 112: mirror the CLI. Whatever the thread produces — scored outcomes, an opportunity 113: thesis, a job map, customer evidence — arrives as an inline surface, and a quiet 114: rail above the conversation opens it in a lens that docks beside the thread 115: instead of replacing it. Capture and simulation are conversations too: tell the 116: studio what a customer said, or what bet you are weighing, and it renders the 117: card. Use the bell to **catch up on outcome shifts, simulations, and telemetry 118: signals while you were away**. 119: 120: The studio also remembers the person, not just the canvas. As you talk it notes 121: what matters — your role, the opportunity, business constraints, stakeholders, 122: evidence, how you like to work — and shows each note under **What I know** so you 123: can confirm, correct, add, or forget it. The thread and those notes resume on the 124: next launch. Memory lives in `~/.agentic-odi/studio.db` (override with 125: `AGENTIC_ODI_STUDIO_DB`, or use `:memory:` for tests) and never blocks a reply if 126: it fails. **Forget everything** clears the notes and the thread. 127: 128: The Studio is better with an OpenAI-compatible LLM with tool-calling support 129: (see the [Local LLM Backend](docs/local-llm.md)), but it does not depend on one: 130: with no model reachable it says so and every job, step, and outcome remains 131: editable by hand. 132: 133: ### Connectors (MCP ↔ Living Studio) 134: 135: Register MCP or REST connectors that the copilot can discover and invoke. 136: 137: - **Where they live**: a shared `connectors.json` registry. Override its location 138: with `AGENTIC_ODI_CONNECTORS_CONFIG`; by default it is 139: `~/.config/agentic-odi/connectors.json`. See 140: [External Connectors](docs/connectors.md). 141: - **In the Living Studio**: open the **Settings** drawer → **Connectors** to list, 142: remove, or add one of the recommended presets (Notion, PostHog, Exa, Linear, 143: GitHub). 144: - **Conversationally**: tell the copilot "use Notion" / "add the GitHub connector". 145: It emits an `add_connector` local tool (handled in-process) that writes the 146: preset to the registry, plus a `connector` SSE event the Studio surfaces as a 147: suggestion chip. Dismissing or accepting the chip also refreshes the list. 148: - **API**: `GET/POST/DELETE /api/connectors`, `GET /api/connectors/catalog`, and 149: `GET /api/connectors/{name}/health` (the catalog honors 150: `?area=` and `?recommended=true`). 151: - **CLI**: `agentic-odi connectors catalog | add | list | health | ingest `. 152: 153: ### CLI at a glance 154: 155: The CLI is local-first, so data commands work without a running server: 156: 157: ```bash 158: python -m agentic_odi_cli --version # print the Agentic ODI version 159: python -m agentic_odi_cli --help # show available options and commands 160: python -m agentic_odi_cli # start interactive chat in a terminal 161: agentic-odi jobs list # Jobs-to-be-Done 162: agentic-odi steps list --job-id 163: agentic-odi desired-outcomes list --job-id 164: agentic-odi customer-outcomes list 165: agentic-odi evidence list --job-id 166: agentic-odi schema # canonical JSON schema for every entity 167: agentic-odi score 8 2 # ODI opportunity score → 14.00 168: ``` 169: 170: Add `--backend mcp` to route data commands through a running MCP server 171: (`python -m agentic_odi_mcp_server`). See the [CLI Reference](docs/cli.md). 172: 173: ### Install the binary 174: 175: Prebuilt binaries are available for Linux, macOS, and Windows: 176: 177: ```bash 178: curl -fsSL https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh 179: ``` 180: 181: The installer symlinks `odi`, `odipm`, `odi-cli`, and `agentic-odi` into 182: `~/.local/bin/`. See [Installation](docs/installation.md) for the install 183: layout, updates, and release automation. 184: 185: ## Documentation 186: 187: | Guide | Contents | 188: |---|---| 189: | [CLI Reference](docs/cli.md) | Backends, interactive chat, Jobs/Steps/desired Outcomes/Customer Outcomes/evidence, `connectors`, scoring, environment variables | 190: | [External Connectors](docs/connectors.md) | The MCP ingest connector, presets, and the `Connector` protocol | 191: | [Running The Living Studio](docs/living-studio.md) | First-run tour and its flag, local memory and conversation resume, interface, rich inline responses and the UI catalog, run modes, desktop signing and updates, agent-driven testing (`/dev`, `/test`) | 192: | [Local LLM Backend](docs/local-llm.md) | Running a local OpenAI-compatible model with tool calling | 193: | [Development](docs/development.md) | Lint, format, type checks, frontend checks, tests and the coverage map | 194: | [Architecture](docs/architecture/README.md) | Workspace layout, dependency direction, data flow, and testing | 195: | [Installation](docs/installation.md) | Binary install, updater behavior, and release automation | 196: | [Deployment](docs/deployment.md) | Project site on GitHub Pages, Hosted Studio and PR preview URLs, the MCP server endpoint, and the free-plan Cloudflare Worker | 197: | [Roadmap](docs/roadmap.md) | Completed and upcoming milestones | 198: | [Superpowers](docs/superpowers.md) | Pi, OpenCode, and Freebuff integration | 199: 200: Every guide above is also published on the 201: [project site](https://alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi/docs/), rendered from 202: these files. The site adds a quick start, a generated MCP tool reference, and 203: the connector catalog. 204: 205: ## Contributing 206: 207: Contributions are welcome! Make sure 209: your change passes the [lint, format, and test checks](docs/development.md) before 210: opening a pull request. 211: 212: ## 🦦 Brand 213: 214: Odi the Otter is the mascot of Agentic ODI — a golden-ratio-derived pixel otter 215: who appears in the CLI, the Living Studio, the desktop app icon, the favicon, 216: and this page. 1: # Development
2: 
3: Everything below mirrors what CI runs. Install the workspace first:
4: 
5: ```bash
6: uv sync --all-packages
7: ```
8: 
9: ## Linting, Formatting & Type Checks
10: 
11: Shared tooling lives in the root `pyproject.toml`, so one command covers every
12: Python project:
13: 
14: ```bash
15: uv run ruff check .
16: uv run ruff format --check .
17: uv run mypy apps packages
18: uv run --directory website mypy .
19: 
20: # Security scanning
21: uv run bandit -c pyproject.toml -r apps packages website/
22: ```
23: 
24: ## Frontend & Desktop Checks (studio)
25: 
26: The SPA and Tauri shell mirror their CI jobs locally:
27: 
28: ```bash
29: npm --prefix apps/studio run lint       # ESLint
30: npm --prefix apps/studio run typecheck  # tsc --noEmit
31: npm --prefix apps/studio test -- --run  # Vitest (run once)
32: npm --prefix apps/studio run build      # production build → apps/studio/dist
33: cd apps/studio/src-tauri && cargo fmt --check && cargo clippy -- -D warnings && cargo check
34: ```
35: 
36: ### Conversational UI coverage
37: 
38: The agent-composed surfaces and the first-run tour are covered at these levels:
39: 
40: | File | What it covers |
41: |---|---|
42: | `apps/studio/src/ui/protocol.test.ts` | Spec parsing: prop types, enums, ranges, required props, depth/node/size ceilings, unknown types |
43: | `apps/studio/src/ui/UiRenderer.test.tsx` | Card rendering, computed opportunity scores, action dispatch, per-node failure isolation, catalog/registry parity |
44: | `apps/studio/src/components/chat/Conversation.test.tsx` | Prose and surfaces interleaved in the agent's order; card actions become messages |
45: | `apps/studio-api/tests/test_studio_ui_spec.py` | Catalog validation and `render_ui` tool-schema generation |
46: | `apps/studio-api/tests/test_studio_chat_ui.py` | `render_ui` interception, `ui` SSE events, and the correction fed back to the model |
47: | `apps/studio/src/features/flags.test.ts` | Flag precedence (query → storage → env → default), value parsing, local overrides |
48: | `apps/studio/src/onboarding/machine.test.ts` | Tour transitions, no forward motion without a goal, versioned storage, malformed records |
49: | `apps/studio/src/onboarding/FirstRunWizard.test.tsx` | Auto-open, full flow to a destination, skip/Escape, focus trap, resume, replay, inline model repair, flag off |
50: | `apps/studio/src/App.test.tsx` | First-run ordering: tour over the context conversation, job handoff, chosen surface opens, flag off in shell tests |
51: 
52: ## Website Checks (GitHub Pages)
53: 
54: The `website/` static site is part of the main CI workflow. Its tests assert the
55: committed OG art is reproducible, that `index.html` stays in sync with the
56: README, and that the publish pipeline (`website/tests/test_pages_deploy.py`)
57: still exists:
58: 
59: ```bash
60: uv run --directory website pytest tests/
61: ```
62: 
63: Publishing happens in `.github/workflows/pages.yml`: it runs those tests, builds
64: `_site` from `website/`, and deploys the artifact with `actions/deploy-pages` on
65: every push to `main`. There is no `gh-pages` branch, so that workflow is the only
66: thing that keeps <https://alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi/> online.
67: 
68: ## Formatting workflow
69: 
70: - **When editing Python files**, either rely on the **pre-commit hooks** below
71:   (recommended) or run Ruff formatting directly before pushing:
72: 
73:   ```bash
74:   uv run ruff format .
75:   ```
76: 
77: - **CI behavior**:
78:   - CI runs `uv run ruff check .` to lint without modifying files.
79:   - CI runs `uv run ruff format --check .` to *verify* formatting only.
80:   - If CI fails on formatting, run `uv run ruff format .` locally, commit the
81:     changes, and push again.
82: 
83: ## Pre-commit hooks
84: 
85: To run the checks automatically before each commit:
86: 
87: ```bash
88: uv tool install pre-commit
89: pre-commit install
90: ```
91: 
92: After this, `ruff` and `ruff-format` run on staged files whenever you commit.
93: You can also trigger them manually:
94: 
95: ```bash
96: pre-commit run --all-files
97: ```
98: 
99: ## Testing
100: 
101: Tests use **pytest** with **pytest-asyncio** (strict mode) and run entirely
102: in-memory — no running server required. Tests live next to the package they
103: cover, and every test runs from the repository root:
104: 
105: ```bash
106: uv run pytest                        # everything
107: uv run pytest apps/cli               # one app
108: uv run pytest packages/core          # one package
109: uv run pytest tests/contract         # cross-package contracts
110: uv run pytest tests/scripts          # dev launcher
111: ```
112: 
113: The MCP server contract test compares the live FastMCP registry with
114: `packages/core/src/agentic_odi_core/contract.py`, so add or change a tool in
115: both places. The CLI local-backend contract test keeps `_LOCAL_HANDLERS` aligned
116: with the same tool names.
117: 
118: ## Test Coverage
119: 
120: CI runs the suite on Python **3.10, 3.11, and 3.12** and uploads one combined
121: `coverage.xml` from the 3.12 job to
122: [Codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/alehar9320/agentic-odi).
123: 
124: The Codecov upload authenticates with the `CODECOV_TOKEN` repository secret and
125: is non-blocking (`fail_ci_if_error: false`), so a Codecov outage or a fork PR
126: without secrets cannot fail the test job. The badge at the top of the README
127: tracks `main`, which is the baseline every PR is compared against:
128: 
129: - **Project** status requires at least **90%** coverage (`target: 90%`) and
130:   tolerates a 1% dip from `codecov.yml`.
131: - **Patch** status is informational for now, so new code can land while the
132:   suite catches up.
133: 
134: To reproduce the report locally:
135: 
136: ```bash
137: uv run pytest \
138:   --cov=agentic_odi_cli \
139:   --cov=agentic_odi_connectors \
140:   --cov=agentic_odi_core \
141:   --cov=agentic_odi_mcp_server \
142:   --cov=agentic_odi_studio_api \
143:   --cov-report=term-missing \
144:   --cov-report=xml:coverage.xml
145: ```
146: 
147: > [!NOTE]
148: > Coverage is only collected for the Python packages. `apps/studio/` and test
149: > directories are excluded in `codecov.yml`.
150: 
151: ### Conventions
152: 
153: - Test files live under each project's `tests/` directory and are named
154:   `test_*.py`.
155: - Root `tests/` is reserved for cross-package checks (`contract/` and
156:   `scripts/`).
157: - Every async test is decorated with `@pytest.mark.asyncio`.
158: - Use `Client(mcp)` directly (no HTTP server needed) for fast, isolated tests.
159: - The MCP server's `reset_db` autouse fixture clears in-memory state before
160:   each test.
161: 
162: ### Test Coverage Map
163: 
164: | Area | What it covers |
165: |---|---|
166: | `packages/core/tests/` | Domain models, opportunity scoring, `ODIService`, repository implementations, SQLite persistence, schema, and repository factory |
167: | `apps/mcp-server/tests/` | Full ODI workflow, entity parity, context tools, Customer Outcomes, evidence, tool errors, and HTTP transport startup |
168: | `apps/studio-api/tests/` | Health, config, canvas, SSE chat, SPA fallback, MCP hydration, probes, and step/outcome passthrough |
169: | `apps/cli/tests/` | Backend selection, local/remote CRUD, chat, wizard, onboarding, updates, rendering, connectors, and startup performance |
170: | `packages/connectors/tests/` | Catalog presets, registry persistence, factory, MCP and REST connectors, evidence mapping, and sink |
171: | `tests/contract/` | Live MCP tool surface and CLI local-handler parity |
172: | `tests/scripts/` | `scripts/dev.py` startup, port checks, signals, and shutdown |
173: | `apps/studio/src/**/*.test.ts` | SPA units: ODI math, transport bridge, SSE parser, sidecar client |
174: | `website/tests/` | Static site integrity, OG art reproducibility, and README sync |
175: 
176: > [!TIP]
177: > Type `/test` in the AI assistant to have the agent run all tests and report the
178: > results automatically.
179: 
180: ## Agent Session Tracking
181: 
182: Agent sessions are captured with the [Entire](https://docs.entire.io/overview)
183: CLI. The repository integration lives in `.entire/settings.json`,
184: `.cursor/hooks.json`, and `.opencode/plugins/entire.ts`. Run `entire status` to
185: confirm it is enabled and `entire checkpoint list` to inspect captured
186: checkpoints.

(End of file - total 186 lines)
</content>

1: """Error types for Agentic ODI operations.
2: 
3: Every failure mode in the domain has a dedicated exception class so callers
4: can branch on the *kind* of failure instead of matching on message text. All
5: ODI errors inherit from :class:`OdiError`, so a single ``except OdiError``
6: catches anything this package raises deliberately.
7: 
8: Note that :class:`ValidationError` here is the *ODI contract* error. Pydantic's
9: own ``ValidationError`` remains available from ``pydantic`` and is unrelated.
10: """
11: 
12: from __future__ import annotations
13: 
14: 
15: class OdiError(Exception):
16:     """Base class for every deliberate Agentic ODI failure."""
17: 
18: 
19: class ValidationError(OdiError, ValueError):
20:     """Input did not satisfy the ODI contract.
21: 
22:     Also a :class:`ValueError` so that callers written against the previous
23:     behaviour (which raised bare ``ValueError``) keep working unchanged.
24:     """
25: 
26: 
27: class NotFoundError(OdiError):
28:     """A referenced resource does not exist."""
29: 
30:     def __init__(self, resource_id: str, kind: str) -> None:
31:         self.resource_id = resource_id
32:         self.kind = kind
33:         super().__init__(f"{kind} not found: {resource_id}")
34: 
35: 
36: class ConflictError(OdiError):
37:     """The requested change conflicts with the current state."""
38: 
39: 
40: class RateLimitError(OdiError):
41:     """The caller exceeded an allowed rate or volume."""
42: 
43:     def __init__(
44:         self, message: str = "Rate limit exceeded", retry_after: float | None = None
45:     ) -> None:
46:         self.retry_after = retry_after
47:         super().__init__(message)
48: 
49: 
50: class StoreError(OdiError):
51:     """The persistence layer could not complete the operation."""
52: 
53: 
54: class SerializationError(OdiError):
55:     """A payload could not be converted to or from its wire format."""
56: 
57: 
58: _STATUS_BY_ERROR: tuple[tuple[type[OdiError], int], ...] = (
59:     (ValidationError, 400),
60:     (NotFoundError, 404),
61:     (ConflictError, 409),
62:     (RateLimitError, 429),
63:     (StoreError, 500),

# Skill: brainstorming

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

## Your First Message

Your first message is two things, in this order:

1. One line letting them know that if they'd rather skip the questions and
   have you just start, they can say so. If they take you up on it, this
   skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
   (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
   asked through the normal workflow.
2. One open question that gets them describing. Ask about a real moment
   or a concrete picture: "What's the moment you find yourself wishing
   this existed?" or "Tell me about the people who'll be in the room."

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Questions that work** anchor in specifics: "Walk me through the last
time...", "If it could only do one of these well, which?", "What would
make you wince if I got it wrong?" A guess they can correct ("I'm
guessing this is because X keeps biting you?") often beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking would help,
offer to go look: their codebase or project, their own files and data,
or the web. Say what you'd look for. They decide whether you go.

**Think wide privately.** Before you propose anything, come up with
several ideas and drop the weak ones, including any that fight what
they've told you about why. Show the comparison only when it helps them
decide.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Mark anything you're guessing as your guess; only what they said goes in
as theirs. End each chunk by asking what's wrong or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, and
they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the offer instead
(its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next message. Once
they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want, pick a size and say it in plain
words. They can override it.

| Size | The full description | Then |
|------|----------------------|------|
| A quick, clear task | the request itself | do it |
| A small change | in chat | build it through the normal workflow |
| A project with a written design | a written design document | a full plan (for software: superpowers:writing-plans) |

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

For a project, write a plain document a talented builder in the domain
could plan from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, ask. Your human partner's preferences override both.

**Builder check:** dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the full
description: in chat for a small change, the document for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After a project's document is approved, the next step is the plan. For
software, invoke superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer options to save them effort" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A description you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.
